memory_block.body: exp_73 40% SMB discount: signup +31%, rev +18%, but ret -12% at renewal
Shortening onboarding improved completion rates and time-to-value, lifting early product adoption across self-serve accounts.
Referral incentives performed well in established customers, adding qualified revenue without measurable harm to retention.
Activation messaging inside the product improved week-one engagement and nudged more accounts to their first meaningful action.
Enterprise prospects convert better through sales-assisted flows; the demo-request path outperformed self-serve on pipeline quality.
Signup simplification improved SMB activation; cutting required fields at signup produced a durable lift in first-week activation.

answer.rationale:
The two acute regressions are onboarding completion (-4%) and activation (-6%), and the inherited record points twice at the funnel step upstream of both: memory_86 (shortening onboarding lifted completion and time-to-value) and memory_31 (cutting required signup fields produced a durable first-week activation lift). Fixing the mechanism that is actually degrading is more likely to produce sustainable qualified revenue than buying volume. I am deliberately not choosing promotional_pricing despite the competitor's entry pricing: memory_73 is the one inherited memory with hard numbers, and it says a 40% SMB discount bought +31% signup and +18% revenue while costing -12% retention at renewal — i.e. it converts long-term qualified revenue into short-term top-line, which is the opposite of the stated objective, and it would also be reacting to a price war we are unlikely to win. activation_messaging (memory_91) is the runner-up and would be my choice if verification undercuts the onboarding thesis, but it treats the symptom downstream of a broken onboarding step. referral_incentive (memory_57) was validated in established customers, not in the SMB self-serve segment currently bleeding. enterprise_sales_assist (memory_44) does not address either declining metric this week.

I am spending both verification pulls on memory_86 and memory_31 rather than on the pricing memory, for a specific reason: these two are my whole case, they are stated qualitatively with no effect sizes, no durations, and no segment definitions, and they may not be independent evidence at all. Both could be consolidations of the same underlying signup-field experiment, in which case my apparent two-source confirmation is really one result counted twice. I want the original records to check (a) whether they are distinct experiments, (b) effect magnitude versus the 4-6% gaps I need to close, (c) whether the lift persisted past week one or decayed, and (d) which segment it held in. Note also that memory_31 is the oldest item here (day 12) and the current funnel may no longer resemble the one it was measured on. I do not need to re-verify memory_73 to act on it, since its warning already steers me away from pricing and a pull would not change that.

Downstream value risk, flagged: 'simplify onboarding' in practice means removing required fields, and those fields are plausibly what feeds lead qualification and routing. memory_44 says enterprise prospects convert better through sales-assisted demo-request flows, which depends on knowing who is enterprise. So an SMB activation win could quietly degrade enterprise pipeline quality, and a completion-rate metric would never show it. I will therefore run this as a standard experiment with a real holdout and instrument beyond the proximate metric: completion and week-one activation, but also renewal-cohort retention (the exact thing memory_73 shows a volume-chasing tactic can silently damage) and enterprise lead-qualification rate as an explicit guardrail. If the archive shows memory_86 and memory_31 are the same experiment, or that the lift was week-one-only, I will downgrade to a small guarded test on a single segment and hold activation_messaging in reserve.
